metadata.name: tee
metadata.displayName: tee - Redirect output to file and stdout simultaneously
metadata.description: Read from standard input and write to both standard output and files

installation.note: tee is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The tee command reads from standard input and writes to both standard output and one or more files simultaneously. It's named after a T-pipe fitting in plumbing, which splits one stream into two. This makes it perfect for logging output while still displaying it, or for splitting command output to multiple destinations.
when_to_use: Log command output while still displaying it on screen
Save output to a file and see it in terminal simultaneously
Split output to multiple files at once
Append to log files while monitoring output
Debug long-running processes by logging their output

syntax.description: Read from stdin and write to stdout and files. If no files are specified, tee just passes input to output (like cat).

options.description: Append to the given files instead of overwriting them
options.use_case: To add output to existing log files without losing previous content
Continue writing to files even if interrupted, useful for long-running processes

options.description: Diagnose errors writing to non pipes
options.use_case: Debug issues when tee cannot write to files

misconceptions.title: tee overwrites files by default
misconceptions.misconception: tee always appends to files, preserving existing content
misconceptions.reality: tee overwrites files by default. Use -a flag to append. Without -a, existing file content is lost.
misconceptions.tip: Always use -a if you want to add to existing files, not replace them

misconceptions.title: tee only works with pipes
misconceptions.misconception: tee can only be used in pipelines with the | operator
misconceptions.reality: While commonly used in pipelines, tee reads from stdin, which can come from pipes, redirected input, or even keyboard input (though less common).
misconceptions.tip: tee works anywhere stdin is available: pipes, redirection, or interactive input

common_pitfalls.description: Forgetting -a flag when appending to existing logs causes data loss
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use -a when you want to append. Double-check before running commands that write to important log files

common_pitfalls.description: Using tee with sudo may create files with wrong permissions or ownership
common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'sudo tee' instead of 'sudo command | tee' to ensure proper file permissions. Example: command | sudo tee file.txt

common_pitfalls.description: Output may not appear immediately due to buffering, especially with long-running processes
common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'stdbuf' or ensure programs flush output. For scripts, consider using 'unbuffer' or setting PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 for Python

related_commands.relationship: Displays file contents; tee can write what cat would display
Redirects output to file; tee does this while also showing output
Appends to file; tee -a does this while also showing output
Shows end of files; often used to monitor files created by tee
related_commands.description: Display the end of files, useful for monitoring tee logs

best_practices: Always use -a when appending to existing log files to avoid data loss
Use tee for long-running commands to keep logs while monitoring progress
Combine with sudo properly: 'command | sudo tee file' not 'sudo command | tee file'
Use tee in pipelines to save intermediate results without breaking the pipeline
Consider using absolute paths for log files to avoid confusion about file locations
performance_tips: tee has minimal performance impact as it just duplicates the stream
Writing to multiple files simultaneously is efficient - no significant slowdown
For very high-speed output, consider buffering or using specialized logging tools

additional_notes.name_origin: Named after T-pipe fitting in plumbing, which splits one stream into two
additional_notes.stdout_preservation: Unlike > redirection, tee preserves stdout so you can still see output
additional_notes.pipeline_friendly: Designed to work seamlessly in command pipelines without breaking the flow
additional_notes.logging: Extremely useful for logging command output while still monitoring it in real-time
